**Jacquelyn Young** (born September 16, 1997) is an American professional basketball player for the Las Vegas Aces of the Women's National Basketball Association (WNBA). She is the daughter of Linda Young and David Wayne Edwards, Sr. She was drafted first overall by the Las Vegas Aces in the 2019 WNBA draft. A graduate of Princeton Community High School, she played college basketball for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish, reaching two NCAA finals and winning one in 2018. She won a gold medal in Women's 3x3 basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics and a national WNBA championship in 2022.[[1]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-:0-1) In 2024, she won the gold medal in 5x5 basketball at the 2024 Summer Olympics.
In Young's high school career, the PCHS Tigers posted a 97-9 (.915) record. She finished as the leading scorer (girls' or boys' basketball) in Indiana high school history with 3,268 points, eclipsing the 26-year-old record set by Damon Bailey. Overall, Young averaged 30.8 points, 10.3 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 3.5 steals per game, while shooting .583 from the field, .382 from beyond the arc and .858 from the free-throw line. She led Princeton to 53 consecutive wins and the 2015 Indiana Class 3A state championship. She scored 36 points in state title game, setting the record for most points in a Class 3A final, as well as the most points by one player in any Indiana girls' basketball state title game since 1980. It is said that Young gets most of her athletic genes from her father who was a start high school basketball player as well as track athlete. Young also has a brother, David Wayne Edwards, Jr., who was a defensive back for the national championship team of the University of Nebraska in 1997.
texts.2:
Young led her team to a 27–1 record in her senior season, ranking third in the state and ninth in the nation in scoring with 34.9 PPG. She also achieved 9.5 rebounds, 5.0 assists and 3.8 steals. She shot .605 as a senior with a .429 mark from three-point range and an .861 free-throw percentage. All told, she compiled 20 30-point games, 10 40-point games and a season high 53 points on Nov 20 vs. county rival Gibson Southern. She was the recipient of the 2016 Indiana Miss Basketball award.
Young set the Indiana high school girls' basketball single season scoring record as a junior, recording 1,003 points. She was the fifth player of either sex in state history to score 1,000 points in a season. She was ranked in the top-10 by nearly all major national recruiting services, including a No. 5 rank by Prospects Nation.
Young played three seasons of college basketball for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish between 2016 and 2019, where she won an NCAA championship as a sophomore in 2018.[[2]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-3) She earned ACC All-Freshman Team in 2017 and second-team All-ACC in 2019. She also earned ACC tournament MVP in 2019.[[4]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-usbasket-4)
texts.3:
Young had the option to remain at Notre Dame for the 2019–20 college season, but opted to enter the 2019 WNBA draft where she was selected with the first overall pick by the Las Vegas Aces, coached by Bill Laimbeer.[[5]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-5) She later signed a multi-year deal with Puma.[[6]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-m022-6) She played the 2019 WNBA season as a point guard for the first time, having played as a shooting guard in college.[[7]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-poised-for-breakout-7) Young finished eighth in the WNBA with 153 total assists, and her 2.89 assist/turnover ranked sixth overall. She averaged 6.6 points and 3.3 rebounds per game[[7]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-poised-for-breakout-7) and was subsequently named to the WNBA All-Rookie Team.[[8]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-8)
In the 2020 WNBA season, Young averaged 10.1 points, 4.0 rebounds and 3.0 assist in 40 games with the Aces.[[4]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-usbasket-4)

**Jacquelyn Young** (born September 16, 1997) is an American professional basketball player for the Las Vegas Aces of the Women's National Basketball Association (WNBA). She is the daughter of Linda Young and David Wayne Edwards, Sr. She was drafted first overall by the Las Vegas Aces in the 2019 WNBA draft. A graduate of Princeton Community High School, she played college basketball for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish, reaching two NCAA finals and winning one in 2018. She won a gold medal in Women's 3x3 basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics and a national WNBA championship in 2022.[[1]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-:0-1) In 2024, she won the gold medal in 5x5 basketball at the 2024 Summer Olympics.
In Young's high school career, the PCHS Tigers posted a 97-9 (.915) record. She finished as the leading scorer (girls' or boys' basketball) in Indiana high school history with 3,268 points, eclipsing the 26-year-old record set by Damon Bailey. Overall, Young averaged 30.8 points, 10.3 rebounds, 5.5 assists and 3.5 steals per game, while shooting .583 from the field, .382 from beyond the arc and .858 from the free-throw line. She led Princeton to 53 consecutive wins and the 2015 Indiana Class 3A state championship. She scored 36 points in state title game, setting the record for most points in a Class 3A final, as well as the most points by one player in any Indiana girls' basketball state title game since 1980. It is said that Young gets most of her athletic genes from her father who was a start high school basketball player as well as track athlete. Young also has a brother, David Wayne Edwards, Jr., who was a defensive back for the national championship team of the University of Nebraska in 1997.

Young led her team to a 27–1 record in her senior season, ranking third in the state and ninth in the nation in scoring with 34.9 PPG. She also achieved 9.5 rebounds, 5.0 assists and 3.8 steals. She shot .605 as a senior with a .429 mark from three-point range and an .861 free-throw percentage. All told, she compiled 20 30-point games, 10 40-point games and a season high 53 points on Nov 20 vs. county rival Gibson Southern. She was the recipient of the 2016 Indiana Miss Basketball award.
Young set the Indiana high school girls' basketball single season scoring record as a junior, recording 1,003 points. She was the fifth player of either sex in state history to score 1,000 points in a season. She was ranked in the top-10 by nearly all major national recruiting services, including a No. 5 rank by Prospects Nation.
Young played three seasons of college basketball for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish between 2016 and 2019, where she won an NCAA championship as a sophomore in 2018.[[2]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-3) She earned ACC All-Freshman Team in 2017 and second-team All-ACC in 2019. She also earned ACC tournament MVP in 2019.[[4]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-usbasket-4)

Young had the option to remain at Notre Dame for the 2019–20 college season, but opted to enter the 2019 WNBA draft where she was selected with the first overall pick by the Las Vegas Aces, coached by Bill Laimbeer.[[5]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-5) She later signed a multi-year deal with Puma.[[6]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-m022-6) She played the 2019 WNBA season as a point guard for the first time, having played as a shooting guard in college.[[7]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-poised-for-breakout-7) Young finished eighth in the WNBA with 153 total assists, and her 2.89 assist/turnover ranked sixth overall. She averaged 6.6 points and 3.3 rebounds per game[[7]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-poised-for-breakout-7) and was subsequently named to the WNBA All-Rookie Team.[[8]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-8)
In the 2020 WNBA season, Young averaged 10.1 points, 4.0 rebounds and 3.0 assist in 40 games with the Aces.[[4]](https://wnba.miraheze.org/wiki/Jackie_Young#cite_note-usbasket-4)

The **UConn Huskies women's basketball** team is the college basketball program representing the University of Connecticut in Storrs, Connecticut, in the NCAA Division I women's basketball competition. They currently play in the Big East Conference.

The UConn Huskies have won a record 12 NCAA Division I National Championships and a women's record four in a row, from 2013 through 2016,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-Fox_Sports-2) plus over 50 conference regular season and tournament championships. They have taken part in every [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") since [1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "1989 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"); as of the end of the 2024–25 season, this is the second-longest active streak in Division I.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-3) From 2008 to 2022, they appeared in a record 14 consecutive Final Fours.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-Final_Fours-4)
UConn owns the two longest winning streaks (men's or women's) in college basketball history.

The longest streak, 111 straight wins, started with a win against Creighton University on November 23, 2014, and ended on March 31, 2017, when a buzzer-beater at the end of overtime caused a 66–64 loss in the [2017 NCAA Final Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2017 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") to [Mississippi State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Mississippi_State_Bulldogs_women's_basketball_team "2016–17 Mississippi State Bulldogs women's basketball team").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-5) The second streak counts 90 consecutive wins, including two undefeated seasons (2008–09 and 2009–10), and was delimited by two losses against Stanford, the first on April 6, 2008, in the National Semifinals of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2008 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), and the second – three seasons later – on December 19, 2010.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-6) The Huskies also own the longest winning streak in regular-season games in college history; after an overtime loss to [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Stanford_Cardinal_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 Stanford Cardinal women's basketball team") on November 17, 2014, they won their next 126 regular-season games until a 68–57 loss to Baylor on January 3, 2019.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-7)

UConn women's basketball has won a record 12 national championships, including back-to-back titles in 2009-10, a three-peat from 2002-04 and four in a row from 2013-16. The Huskies have produced the national player of the year as many times as they have cut down the nets and they're led by arguably the greatest coach of all-time.
With a victory over FDU on November 20, 2024, Geno Auriemma secured his 1,217th career win, setting the NCAA record for the most career victories by any coach in college basketball history.
Here's everything you need to know about the UConn women's basketball dynasty, including season-by-season records, the school's all-time roster and breakdowns of every one of the Huskies' championships.

## UConn women's basketball stats, records
Video 5
Here are some of the most impressive stats and records from the UConn dynasty.
*   The Huskies have had six undefeated seasons, including two in three years (2013-14 and 2015-16)and back-to-back undefeated seasons in 2008-09 and 2009-10. They've also had six one-loss seasons.  
*   Since 1995, UConn has had the AP National Player of the Year 12 times. The Huskies have produced the ESPY-winning Best Female College Athlete nine times and coach Geno Auriemma has been named AP National Coach of the Year nine times.  
*   The AP National Player of the Year award winners: Rebecca Lobo (1995), Jennifer Rizzotti (1996),Kara Wolters (1997), Sue Bird (2002),Diana Taurasi (2003), Maya Moore (2009), Tina Charles (2010), Maya Moore again (2011), Breanna Stewart (2014, 2015 and 2016) and Paige Bueckers (2021).  
*   The last time UConn _didn't_ have an AP All-American was in 2007. From 2008 to 2023, the Huskies had 30 All-Americans.  
*   UConn has made 24 Final Four appearances, which is the most of any men's or women's program. The Huskies reached a record of 14 straight Final Fours from 2008 to 2022.  
*   Nykesha Sales has the single-game scoring record: 46 points vs. Stanford on Dec. 21, 1997.  
*   There have been at least 27 games in UConn history in which a player attempted a minimum of six shots and made every shot she took, most notably Rebecca Lobo's 11-for-11 performance against Iona in 1994. Katie Lou Samuelson once set a 3-point record with a 10-for-10 day against USF in 2017.

The **UConn Huskies women's basketball** team is the college basketball program representing the University of Connecticut in Storrs, Connecticut, in the NCAA Division I women's basketball competition. They currently play in the Big East Conference.

The UConn Huskies have won a record 12 NCAA Division I National Championships and a women's record four in a row, from 2013 through 2016,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-Fox_Sports-2) plus over 50 conference regular season and tournament championships. UConn owns the two longest winning streaks (men's or women's) in college basketball history.

The longest streak, 111 straight wins, started with a win against Creighton University on November 23, 2014, and ended on March 31, 2017, when a buzzer-beater at the end of overtime caused a 66–64 loss in the [2017 NCAA Final Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2017 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") to [Mississippi State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Mississippi_State_Bulldogs_women's_basketball_team "2016–17 Mississippi State Bulldogs women's basketball team").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-5) The second streak counts 90 consecutive wins, including two undefeated seasons (2008–09 and 2009–10), and was delimited by two losses against Stanford, the first on April 6, 2008, in the National Semifinals of the [NCAA Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2008 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), and the second – three seasons later – on December 19, 2010.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-6) The Huskies also own the longest winning streak in regular-season games in college history; after an overtime loss to [Stanford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Stanford_Cardinal_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 Stanford Cardinal women's basketball team") on November 17, 2014, they won their next 126 regular-season games until a 68–57 loss to Baylor on January 3, 2019.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball#cite_note-7)

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
[edit]
The 2010s marked the pinnacle of Notre Dame women's basketball. In [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2010–11 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), the Irish became the first team in NCAA tournament history to defeat both Tennessee and [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2010–11 Connecticut Huskies women's basketball team") in the same run, advancing to the championship game before falling 76–70 to [Texas A&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Texas_A&M_Aggies_women's_basketball_team "2010–11 Texas A&M Aggies women's basketball team"). The following year, the Irish repeated the feat of reaching the title game, though they were defeated 80–61 by Baylor.

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
The [2012–13 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2012–13 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team") was a program high: a historic 31–1 record, flawless 16–0 Big East play, and the first Big East Tournament championship achieved with a dramatic 61–59 win over [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2012–13 Connecticut Huskies women's basketball team"). However, the Irish ultimately lost in the National Semifinals to Connecticut 83–65, ending their season with a 35–2 overall record. Transitioning to the ACC in [2013–14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2013–14 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), the Irish reached the national championship game in an undefeated (37–0) campaign, only to succumb 79–58 to [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2013–14 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") (hindered by the loss of one of their top stars, Natalie Achonwa, who had torn her ACL in the Elite Eight).

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
In [2014–15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), Notre Dame again contested for the national title after defeating [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_South_Carolina_Gamecocks_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 South Carolina Gamecocks women's basketball team") in a nail-bitter in the National Semifinals, 66–65. In the national championship game, they fell 63–53 to [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") for the second straight year. The Irish finished with a 36–3 record and were ranked No. 2 nationally across the final polls.

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
The defining highlight of the Fighting Irish's modern history arrived in [2017–18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2017–18 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), when a seven-player roster overcame adversity to win a second national championship; Junior Arike Ogunbowale delivered consecutive buzzer-beaters—first in the National Semifinals to defeat previously undefeated [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2017–18 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") 91–89 in overtime, then in the title game to beat [Mississippi State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Mississippi_State_Bulldogs_women's_basketball_team "2017–18 Mississippi State Bulldogs women's basketball team"), 61–58.
The program returned to the Final Four in the [2018–19 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2018–19 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), defeating [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2018–19 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") in the National Semifinals for a second consecutive year, 81–76. In the championship game, the Irish narrowly lost 82–81 to Baylor in a rematch of the 2012 championship game. Over the 2010s decade, Notre Dame appeared in six national championship games, establishing itself as a consistent national powerhouse.

### Transition and rebuilding (2020–2021)
[edit]
Following Muffet McGraw's retirement in 2020, alumna Niele Ivey—herself a former standout guard and assistant—assumed head coaching duties, becoming the first Black woman to coach any sport at the university. The [2020–21 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2020–21 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team") was shaped by COVID-19 disruptions and developmental priorities. While this stretch lacked postseason milestones, it laid the foundation for the program's resurgence under Ivey's leadership.

### Re-emergence and steady progress (2021–2023)
[edit]
Under Ivey's stewardship, Notre Dame steadily regained national prominence. In [2021–22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), the Irish advanced to the Sweet Sixteen before falling a close 66–63 to #1-seeded [NC State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_NC_State_Wolfpack_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 NC State Wolfpack women's basketball team"). The [2022–23 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team") featured an ACC regular-season title and a 27–6 record, with another trip to the Sweet Sixteen—signaling the return of high-level competitiveness. The Irish lost to #2-seeded [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Maryland_Terrapins_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Maryland Terrapins women's basketball team") in the Sweet Sixteen, 76–59.

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
[edit]
The 2010s marked the pinnacle of Notre Dame women's basketball. In [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2010–11 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), the Irish became the first team in NCAA tournament history to defeat both Tennessee and [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2010–11 Connecticut Huskies women's basketball team") in the same run, advancing to the championship game before falling 76–70 to [Texas A&M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010%E2%80%9311_Texas_A&M_Aggies_women's_basketball_team "2010–11 Texas A&M Aggies women's basketball team"). The following year, the Irish repeated the feat of reaching the title game, though they were defeated 80–61 by Baylor.

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
The [2012–13 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2012–13 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team") was a program high: a historic 31–1 record, flawless 16–0 Big East play, and the first Big East Tournament championship achieved with a dramatic 61–59 win over [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2012–13 Connecticut Huskies women's basketball team"). However, the Irish ultimately lost in the National Semifinals to Connecticut 83–65, ending their season with a 35–2 overall record. Transitioning to the ACC in [2013–14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2013–14 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), the Irish reached the national championship game in an undefeated (37–0) campaign, only to succumb 79–58 to [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013%E2%80%9314_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2013–14 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") (hindered by the loss of one of their top stars, Natalie Achonwa, who had torn her ACL in the Elite Eight).

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
In [2014–15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), Notre Dame again contested for the national title after defeating [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_South_Carolina_Gamecocks_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 South Carolina Gamecocks women's basketball team") in a nail-bitter in the National Semifinals, 66–65. In the national championship game, they fell 63–53 to [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2014–15 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") for the second straight year. The Irish finished with a 36–3 record and were ranked No. 2 nationally across the final polls.

### The golden era: Final Fours, championships, and rivalries (2010–2019)
The defining highlight of the Fighting Irish's modern history arrived in [2017–18](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2017–18 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), when a seven-player roster overcame adversity to win a second national championship; Junior Arike Ogunbowale delivered consecutive buzzer-beaters—first in the National Semifinals to defeat previously undefeated [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2017–18 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") 91–89 in overtime, then in the title game to beat [Mississippi State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_Mississippi_State_Bulldogs_women's_basketball_team "2017–18 Mississippi State Bulldogs women's basketball team"), 61–58.
The program returned to the Final Four in the [2018–19 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2018–19 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), defeating [UConn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_UConn_Huskies_women's_basketball_team "2018–19 UConn Huskies women's basketball team") in the National Semifinals for a second consecutive year, 81–76. In the championship game, the Irish narrowly lost 82–81 to Baylor in a rematch of the 2012 championship game. Over the 2010s decade, Notre Dame appeared in six national championship games, establishing itself as a consistent national powerhouse.

### Transition and rebuilding (2020–2021)
[edit]
Following Muffet McGraw's retirement in 2020, alumna Niele Ivey—herself a former standout guard and assistant—assumed head coaching duties, becoming the first Black woman to coach any sport at the university. The [2020–21 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%9321_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2020–21 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team") was shaped by COVID-19 disruptions and developmental priorities. While this stretch lacked postseason milestones, it laid the foundation for the program's resurgence under Ivey's leadership.

### Re-emergence and steady progress (2021–2023)
[edit]
Under Ivey's stewardship, Notre Dame steadily regained national prominence. In [2021–22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team"), the Irish advanced to the Sweet Sixteen before falling a close 66–63 to #1-seeded [NC State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_NC_State_Wolfpack_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 NC State Wolfpack women's basketball team"). The [2022–23 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Notre Dame Fighting Irish women's basketball team") featured an ACC regular-season title and a 27–6 record, with another trip to the Sweet Sixteen—signaling the return of high-level competitiveness. The Irish lost to #2-seeded [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Maryland_Terrapins_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Maryland Terrapins women's basketball team") in the Sweet Sixteen, 76–59.
